questions.html:
Suppose R is a relation with attributes A1, A2, ... , A6.
How many superkeys R has, if the only keys are A1 and A2?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 5)

Answer is $\boxed{48}$

No. of superkeys due to key A1 = A1 union {all possible subsets of other attributes}
                                                        = 2^5

Similarly due to A2 = 2^5
 

Common super keys covered by A1 and A2 would be =  A1A2 union {all possible subsets of other attributes}
                                                                                               = 2^4

So, total superkeys from A1 and A2 only as key are :

=  |superkeys due to A1| + |superkeys due to A2| - |superkeys due to A1,A2|

=  32 + 32 - 16

=  48

questions.html:
Suppose R is a relation with attributes A1, A2, ... , A6.
How many superkeys R has, if the only keys are $\{\mathrm{A} 1, \mathrm{~A} 2\}$ and $\{\mathrm{A} 3, \mathrm{~A} 4\}$ ?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 2)

As {A1,A2} and {A3,A4} are the two Candidate Keys(CK), for each CK rest of the attributes have two choices eitther to be present along with CK to form a Super Key or the other choice is to be not involved in formation of Superkey.

With {A1,A2}, rest of the each $4$ attributes (A3,A4,A5,A6) has two choices. Hence, we can form $2^4$ superkeys.

Similarly with {A3,A4} we can form $2^4$ superkeys.

The keys which are over counted are the keys containg {A1,A2,A3,A4}, so the number of such keys are $2^2$

Hence, total number of superkeys of $R = 2^4+2^4-2^2=28$

Number of Superkeys containing key $A_1A_2=2^4$  Why? coz each of ${A_3,A_4,A_5,A_6}$ has $2$ choices to either be present in the superkey or not.

Number of Superkeys containing key $A_1A_3 = 2^4$

Using Inclusion-Exclusion principle: 

Number of Superkeys : $2^4+2^4-2^3=24$

questions.html:
We say a set of attributes $X$ is closed (with respect to a given set of FD's) if $\mathrm{X}^{+}=\mathrm{X}$.

For which of the following set of functions dependencies does the relation $R(A, B, C, D)$ has $AB, CD$ as closed sets?

options.html: $A \rightarrow B, B \rightarrow C, C \rightarrow D, D \rightarrow A$
$A \rightarrow B, B \rightarrow A, C \rightarrow A, D \rightarrow A$
$A \rightarrow B, B \rightarrow A, C \rightarrow D, D \rightarrow C$

questions.solution:
Answer: A, D

Selected solution (score: 10)

"Closed" Set of Attributes, Definition:

We say a set of attributes $X$ is closed (with respect to a given set of FD’s) if $X^+ = X.$ (Source: Ullman Book for DBMS)

So, $AB$ is closed iff $(AB)^+ = AB.$

$CD$ is closed iff $(CD)^+ = CD$

So, answer will be Option A & D.

Watch this Beautiful question on this concept: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EU5O_8wH3Xw&t=1157s

questions.html:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets of attributes.
Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.html: If a relation has no attribute that is functionally determined by all the other attributes combined, then the relation has no nontrivial FD's at all.
If $\mathrm{X} \subseteq \mathrm{Y}$, then $\mathrm{X}^+\subseteq \mathrm{Y}^+$ (where the closures are taken with respect to the same set of FD's)
If $A B \rightarrow C$ and $A \rightarrow C$, then $B \rightarrow C$.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

Detailed Video Solution:

Option A: Detailed Video Solution - Ullman Book Question

Option B: Detailed Video Solution - Ullman Book Question

Option C: Detailed Video Solution - Ullman Book Question

Option D: Detailed Video Solution - Ullman Book Question

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Answer is $\boxed{A,B,C}$

A. If a relation has no attribute that is functionally determined by all the other attributes combined, then the relation has no nontrivial FD's at all.

Lets assume we have a Relation with R(A,B,C) with only 1 non-trivial functional dependencies {$A\to B$} , we can extrapolate the FD as $AC\to B$. We can easliy conclude that since the contrapositive if given statemen true , the statement itself becomes true. 

B. If X⊆Y, then X+⊆Y+ (where the closures are taken with respect to the same set of FD's)

This is straightaway true. 

C. $(X^+)^{+} = X^+$

This is true because closure of a set of attributes is equal to closure of clsoure of set of attributes. This property is known as Idempotency of Attribute Closure

D. If AB→C and A→C, then B→C.

This need not be true, if we have $AB\to C$ and $A\to C$ then it need not be the case that $B\to C$ is true. Hence this is false.

questions.html:
Consider a relation with schema $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D})$ and FD's $\mathrm{AB} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{D}$, and $\mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}$.
What are all the nontrivial FD's that follow from the given FD's ? You should restrict yourself to FD's with single attributes on the right side.
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 3)

Consider the given functional dependencies (FDs):
\[
AB \rightarrow C, \quad C \rightarrow D, \quad \text{and} \quad D \rightarrow A.
\]

From these, we can infer:
\[
AB \rightarrow D, \quad C \rightarrow A \quad \text{(Transitivity)}, \quad \text{and} \quad BD \rightarrow C \quad \text{(Pseudo Transitivity)}.
\]

\[
\Rightarrow \text{The FD } AB \rightarrow D \text{ can also be written as } ABC \rightarrow D.
\]
\[
\Rightarrow \text{The FD } C \rightarrow A \text{ can be rewritten as } BC \rightarrow A, \, CD \rightarrow A, \text{ and } BCD \rightarrow A.
\]
\[
\Rightarrow \text{The FD } BD \rightarrow C \text{ can be rewritten as } ABD \rightarrow C \text{ as well.}
\]

This makes a total of 11 FDs (3 given, 3 inferred, and 5 from rewriting the inferred attributes).

Now consider rewriting the given FDs.
\[
C \rightarrow D \text{ is equivalent to } BC \rightarrow D \text{ and } AC \rightarrow D.
\]
\[
\text{and, } D \rightarrow A \text{ is equivalent to } BD \rightarrow A.
\]

So that it makes a total of 11 + 3 = 14 FDs. Please note that attempting systematically and sequentially helps avoid counting duplicate FDs.

questions.html:
In a relational database relation, we say a non-empty set of attributes $\mathrm{X}$ is closed (with respect to a given set of functional dependencies FD) if $X^{+}=X$ (where $X^{+}$is the closure of $X).$ Consider a relation with schema $\mathrm{R}\{\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D})$ and an unknown set of FD's.

If we are told which sets of attributes are closed, we can discover the FD's.

Assume that the only closed sets are $\{\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}\},\{\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}\}$.

Which of the following is/are true for $R?$
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 25)

This is a beautiful question from the Ullman DBMS Book. Find Detailed Video Solution with Many more Variations: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EU5O_8wH3Xw&t=1157s  

First, notice that $\{A\}^{+}$is not $\{A\}$, and since $\{A, B\}^{+}=\{A, B\}$, it must be that $A \rightarrow B$ is an FD . With a similar argument, we have that $B \rightarrow A$ is another fd we must include.

The FDs will be:
$$
\{\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{ABD}, \mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{ABC}, \mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}\} \text {. }
$$
The candidate keys are $C, D$.

Detailed Video Solution with Many more Variations: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EU5O_8wH3Xw&t=1157s

questions.html:
Consider a relation $\mathrm{R}\{\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C})$ such that each attribute functionally determines the other two attributes. Relation R and its FD's have several minimal bases.
Which of the following is/are a minimal base (canonical cover) for FDs of R ?
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C

Selected solution (score: 3)

Detailed Video Solution: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EU5O_8wH3Xw&t=4140s

Answer is option $\boxed{A,B,C}$

Original FD :{ ${ A \to B, A \to C,
B \to A, B \to C,
C \to A, C \to B }$ }

A)  $A \to B, B \to A, B \to C, C \to B$

$\boxed{\text{check for minimal}}$

remove $A \to B$ and using remaining functional dep. find out if we can determine $B$ from $A$.

$A^+ : A \ \times$ NOPE, hence $A \to B$ is not redundant functional dependency.

lets check if $B \to A$ is Redundant.

$B^+ : BC \ \times$ we can't determine $A$ from $B$. hence $B \to A$ is not Redundant.

lets check if $B \to C$ is redundant

$B^+ : BA \ \times$ Not redundant.

lets check if $C \to B$ is redundant.

$C^+ : C \ \times$ NOT Redundant.

Hence This FD set is minimal.

$\boxed{\text{check for cover}}$

$A^+ : ABC$
$B^+ : BCA$
$C^+ : CBA$

which covers the original set of functional dependency.

Hence option A is correct coz its minimal cover of FDs of R.

B) $A \to B, B \to C, C \to A$

$\boxed{\text{check for minimal}}$

yes its minimal.

$\boxed{\text{check for cover}}$

$A^+ : ABC$
$B^+ : BCA$
$C^+ : CAB$

It covers FDs of R.

Hence option B is correct.

C) $A \to C, B \to C, C \to A, C \to B$

$\boxed{\text{check for minimal}}$

$A^+ : A$ , hence $A \to C$ is not Redundant.

$B^+ : B$ , hence $B \to C$ is not Redundant aswell

$C^+ : CB$ , hence $C \to A$ is not redundant aswell

$C^+ : CA$ , hence $C \to B$ is also not Redundant.

Hence this set of FDs are minimal.

$\boxed{\text{check for cover}}$

$A^+ : ACB$ yes, it covers FDs of R.

$B^+ : BCA$

$C^+ : CBA$

Hence option C is correct.

D) $A \to C, B \to C, C \to A$

$\boxed{\text{check for minimal}}$

yes its minimal

$\boxed{\text{check for Cover}}$

$A^+ : AC$ $\rightarrow$ Doesn't determine $B$

$B^+ : BCA$

$C^+ : CA$ $\rightarrow$ Doesn't determine $B$

Hence not a cover of FDs of R.

option D is wrong.
